catalog_citation: Decker, Ken. 2013 [2005]. The Song of Kriol: A Grammar of the Kriol Language of Belize. Electronic (Unicode) edition. Belize City: Belize Kriol Project / SIL International.
catalog_locator: sec. 2.6.1 'Word Level Stress', p. 24 (with fn. 26); cf. sec. 2.6.4 'Sentence Level Stress'
catalog_quote: STRESS in Belize Kriol is identified by a higher PITCH. (Stress is marked with ˈ before the stressed syllable, e.g. /wɑːˈtɑ/ ‘water'.) Pitch refers to a higher or lower tone. Length and loudness, two other features that mark stress in some languages, are not as important in determining stress in BK. Multi-syllable words usually have a stress on one of the syllables. There does not appear to be any consistent pattern to the stress of BK words. Words of non-English origin do not follow a consistent pattern. In some words stress is on the final syllable, e.g. /krɑˈkɑ/ ‘nervous’, /ɡiːˈt͡ʃi/ ‘miserly’, /bofoˈto/ ‘awkward’. However, other words have the stress on the first syllable, e.g. /ˈwɑːsi/ ‘fierce’, /ˈkɑblɑ/ ‘inept worker’, /ˈkoŋkɑs/ ‘housefly’. Words that are shared between BK and English do not follow a consistent pattern. Some of them maintain the same pattern as in English, e.g. /d…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage and fn. 26 are verbatim at sec. 2.6.1, printed p. 24 (p. 33) of the Decker 2013 PDF we hold; the 2.6.4 domain quote is also verbatim. (2) Deciding source: Decker's Song of Kriol is the standard SIL descriptive grammar of Belize Kriol (2005/2006 print, 2013 electronic), first-hand with acoustic text analysis; Glottolog's genuine alternatives are an unpublished 1973 thesis, a 1979 Peace Corps handbook and a 1999 grammar of US-diaspora dialects, and web search found no stress/prosody article, JIPA illustration or instrumental study (a 2021 report of Gooden's creole-prosody plenary notes the gap explicitly). (3) downloaded Escure 2013 (APiCS survey): 'Primary stress is often assigned to the final syllable.. Tone appears to play a role in differentiating certain pairs of words' -- a tendency plus an open tone question, no predictable rule, so it refines r

sources.citation: Escure, Geneviève. 2013. Belizean Creole. In Michaelis, S.M., Maurer, P., Haspelmath, M. & Huber, M. (eds.), The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages, vol. 1. Oxford: OUP. Online version: APiCS Online survey chapter 9.
sources.quote: 'Sentential stress is more evenly distributed across syllables, and thus the prosodic contour of the sentence is totally unlike that of the lexifier. Primary stress is often assigned to the final syllable traból ‘trouble,’ aksidén ‘accident.’ Tone appears to play a role in differentiating certain pairs of words, but research remains to be done in this area.'
sources.locator: sec. 4 (Phonology), final paragraph, immediately before sec. 5 'Noun phrase'
sources.note: Only other modern first-hand phonology statement; reports a final-syllable tendency ('often') and possible lexical tone that Decker does not mention -- worth citing as a secondary note on the record, does not change lexical.

tone.quote: Tone is often an important element of the a languages phonology, therefore the linguist should investigate syllabic tone, word level tone and higher level suprasegmental features to see if there is something that needs to be indicated in the orthography. ... Belize Kriol uses intonation as a device for marking certain syntactic relationships for which English uses inflections. There may need to be some way to mark this in a text. The examples above show how intonation clarifies otherwise similar Belize Kriol sentences in which English would use different words or structures.
